title: Compute with numbers
summary: If score starts at 6, what does score <- score * 3 store?
explanation: For numbers in R, + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies.
On the right of an assignment, R computes the expression before changing the name on the left.
score <- score + 2 therefore uses the old score to calculate its replacement.
This lesson uses single numbers. R also supports sequences of values called vectors, whose behavior is a later topic.

```r
score <- 5
score <- score + 2
print(score)
```
Expected result: [1] 7. Follow the instructions in order; this is a worked example, not an in-app execution.

title: Logical vectors and scalar conditions
summary: Replace the right operand TRUE with FALSE. What prints?
explanation: c(TRUE,FALSE) is a two-element logical vector. NA can represent an unknown logical value.
& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

if needs one non-missing logical result. A scalar numeric value can be coerced to logical, but explicit comparisons make intent clearer. It does not choose a policy for an entire vector or an unknown value.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
flags <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
cat(flags & TRUE, sep=",")
```

title: Logical indexing with missing values
summary: Add the explicit !is.na(values) & check to the mask. What prints?
explanation: A mask from values > 2 selects elements whose comparison is TRUE. A comparison involving NA normally produces NA.
Indexing an atomic vector with an NA mask entry includes a missing result at that position. Unknown does not silently mean false.

is.na(values) marks missing entries. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(1, NA, 4)
cat(values[values > 2], sep=",")
```

title: NA NaN and infinite values
summary: Replace is.na with is.finite. What prints?
explanation: NA represents missing information. NaN represents an undefined numeric result. Inf and -Inf represent positive and negative infinity.
is.na is TRUE for NA and NaN, but FALSE for Inf and ordinary finite values. Comparing a value with NA does not establish whether it is missing.
is.finite is TRUE only for finite numeric values, so it is FALSE for NA, NaN and infinities.

title: For loops and safe sequences
summary: Replace values with numeric(0). What prints?
explanation: for (index in seq_along(values)) visits each valid position of this vector. It does not require a separate manual counter update.
seq_along(numeric(0)) is an empty index sequence. The colon operator makes a sequence including both endpoints. Thus 1:length(values) becomes 1:0 for empty input, which is not an empty sequence.
numeric(length(values)) can allocate a result vector before a loop. Avoid repeatedly growing large vectors without measuring the cost.
count <- count + 1 updates the local count once per iteration. The starting zero remains zero if the sequence is empty.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(2, 4)
count <- 0
for (index in seq_along(values)) {
  count <- count + 1
}
cat(count)
```
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: Lazy arguments and force
summary: Insert force(x) as the first statement of choose. What happens for the same call?
explanation: A supplied function argument is usually a promise: its expression and calling environment are retained until the value is needed. An unused argument can therefore contain an expression that would fail if evaluated. stop(message) raises an error and interrupts normal execution.
force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
choose <- function(x, use) {
  if (use) x else 7
}
cat(choose(stop("evaluated"), FALSE), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: List apply and type-stable vapply
summary: Replace sum with function(x) x, keeping numeric(1). What happens?
explanation: lapply returns one list element per input element, preserving a list result even when values are simple. vapply additionally requires each function result to match an explicit length and compatible type template.

numeric(1) is a length-one double template here. Each sum returns one numeric total. vapply may promote compatible simpler types, but it rejects an incompatible result length or type rather than silently choosing a different output shape as sapply can.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- list(c(1, 2), c(4, 5))
result <- vapply(values, sum, numeric(1))
cat(result, "\n")
```

title: Regular expressions and replacements
summary: Remove fixed = TRUE from both calls. What prints?
explanation: grepl returns one logical match result per input string. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; without it, dot is a regular-expression wildcard matching a character. Know which interpretation your input needs.

gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.

title: Namespaces libraries and package boundaries

title: Spread quantiles and units
summary: If every value is multiplied by 2, what happens to sd and IQR?
explanation: sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var is its square and has squared units. quantile estimates cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.

IQR is the difference between upper and lower quartiles. Multiplying all observations by a constant scales sd and IQR by its absolute value and variance by its square. For very small samples, spread estimates are unstable and conventions matter. Removing missing values changes the observations summarized and must follow a stated policy, not merely silence NA output.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
cat(sprintf("%.1f", sd(x)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("%.1f", IQR(x, type = 7)), "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: 1.0
1.0. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: Logistic models and link scales
summary: If type becomes link, is the printed -1.099 a negative probability?
explanation: glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.

predict(type = "response") converts the linear predictor to probabilities, while type = "link" returns log-odds here. This intercept-only example estimates one shared probability. Separation, convergence, sample size and calibration matter in real models; four synthetic outcomes cannot validate risk predictions.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(success = c(0, 0, 0, 1))
fit <- glm(success ~ 1, data = data, family = binomial())
value <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(row = 1), type = "response")
cat(sprintf("%.3f", value), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: 0.250. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: Profiling and measured optimization
summary: If n changes to 100, which claim is supported?
explanation: system.time evaluates an expression and reports measured CPU and elapsed time. Rprof samples execution for profiling, and Rprof(NULL) stops profiling. Short work may produce no useful samples; timings vary by runtime, load and hardware, so this example never asserts a specific duration or speedup.

Profiling identifies where time is spent, not which result is correct. Compare outputs and representative workloads before changing algorithms; warm-up and repeated measurements may matter. This bounded example writes a local profile file and verifies only the computed result plus a nonnegative elapsed measurement.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
measure <- function(n) {
  Rprof("profile.out")
  on.exit(Rprof(NULL), add = TRUE)
  timing <- system.time(total <- sum(seq_len(n)))
  cat(total, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(timing[["elapsed"]] >= 0, "\n", sep = "")
}
measure(1000)

```

Expected output or behavior: 500500
TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Avoid current-clock assertions, and distinguish elapsed duration from calendar-day arithmetic. Ruby Time also has mutating conversions such as localtime; do not assume every time API is immutable.

```ruby
local = instant.getlocal("-05:00")
puts instant.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
puts local.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")

```

title: Command-line arguments and option parsing
summary: If the allowed range is narrowed to 1..10 with the same --minutes 15, what prints?
explanation: ARGV is the array of command-line argument strings. require "optparse" loads OptionParser; on("--minutes N", Integer) declares a value-bearing option and requests integer conversion. parse! consumes recognized options, leaving positional arguments in ARGV.

For this example run ruby main.rb --minutes 15. A parsed integer can still be outside 1..60, and unexpected positional arguments are rejected. OptionParser::ParseError covers malformed or unknown options; neither option parsing nor shell quoting is permission to evaluate user text.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
require "optparse"
minutes = nil
parser = OptionParser.new do |options|
  options.on("--minutes N", Integer) { |value| minutes = value }
end
begin
  parser.parse!(ARGV)
  if ARGV.empty? && minutes && (1..60).cover?(minutes)
    puts minutes
  else
    puts "invalid minutes"
  end
rescue OptionParser::ParseError
  puts "invalid option"
end

```
Expected output or behavior: 15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

title: Threads joining and failure propagation
summary: If the worker raises ArgumentError, "worker failed" instead of returning 22, what happens at join?
explanation: Thread.new starts a concurrent block. join waits for its termination; value waits and returns the block result. Do not let the main program exit while required workers remain unfinished, and do not infer scheduling order from thread creation order.

A failed worker exception is re-raised to code joining or reading its value, so handle it deliberately. Thread.current.report_on_exception = false disables the automatic background diagnostic for this owned worker, not the exception itself; join still re-raises it. The worked case has no worker failure and prints only after joining. Interpreter scheduling and the GVL do not promise faster CPU execution or replace synchronization.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
worker = Thread.new do
  Thread.current.report_on_exception = false
  20 + 2
end
worker.join
puts worker.value

```
Expected output or behavior: 22. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
